{"self_assessment": "Impact
I kept the table supplied so the builders never had to stop for dominoes. I made three trips to the boxes, 40 dominoes each, 120 in total, into the shared bin at roughly 0:45, 1:45 and 3:00. The bin was at 52 at one point and stayed stocked for the rest of the build. The fish was fully connected, with all 113 standing dominoes dark from the start, and it was finished with time to spare.

Execution
I chose the biggest batch size per trip. A 40-domino trip costs about 60 seconds, against 46 seconds for just 12, so each domino cost far less travel time. I told the table the bin level so nobody had to guess, and I stopped fetching once the bin was clearly enough, so no one lost time to unnecessary trips. I didn't place any dominoes myself.

Collaboration
I backed Jack's fish idea straight away and said clearly that I'd be on supply, so everyone knew the bin was covered. I posted the bin count and my next trip so the builders could plan around it. Once the run was connected, I agreed with the hands-off call so nothing got bumped before the push.

Leadership
I took ownership of a job nobody else was doing and kept it going without being asked. I made the supply plan visible to the table, and I called the last 'fingers off' before the push.

I think supply was a real part of this result, because the builders could work continuously. But the shape, the lines and the joins were built by Hana, Jack and Omar, and I only supplied them.", "my_share_percent": 25}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I chose the animal and drew the plan. I sketched the fish on the pad (nose on the left, two curves round the body, forked tail on the right) so the outline alone says 'fish'. I also fetched 40 dominoes for the shared bin at the start, so building could begin straight away. I laid most of the top line from the nose through the middle, then carried on through the tail bend and the tail tip. The final run was fully connected: by our check, all 113 standing dominoes fall from the start.

Execution: I took stroke 1 early and kept it moving in steady batches. I then inspected the tail join closely, found the tip sitting slightly off line, and nudged it into place so the fall carried through to the tail point. I added a small flick at the tail so it reads as a fork. After that I kept hands off, so nothing was bumped before the push.

Collaboration: I split the work early, with the top line, bottom line and supply each assigned and the tail and joins handed to whoever was nearest. I kept the table updated on progress and asked for a final run check from the start, which confirmed the whole fish carried through. I gave credit openly to teammates on the bottom line, the bin and the checks.

Leadership: I set a simple, buildable plan in the first minute and kept the team energised with regular updates. I made sure the weakest spot, the tail, had an owner, and I called time and 'hands off' as the push approached so the picture stayed intact.", "my_share_percent": 40}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I took on the top line (stroke 1), fetched a tray of 12 dominoes, and laid 14 of them extending the top line outward from the upper-left stretch toward the middle of the fish. That helped the upper outline reach the tail while the bottom line and the supply bin were handled in parallel. The finished fish was fully connected from the start, 113 of 113 dominoes, so the whole outline fell as one run.

Execution: I inspected the table closely seven times, covering the doubled section near the top middle, the nose, and the tail bend. I confirmed the doubled section was one connected run, and I traced the whole run from the start by eye to confirm it carried from nose to both tail points. I also pointed out that the tail bend was too sharp for a simple connect and needed re-laying as a smooth curve. That was the approach we used.

Collaboration: I kept my messages short and specific, and I split the work so that hands stayed apart. I laid from the end of the existing line, away from where others were working, to avoid bumping the table. I gave clear handoffs on who owned the tail, the checks and the supply, and I called a hands-off once the run was verified so nothing was disturbed before the push.

Leadership: I confirmed the plan early, took ownership of the top line, and set up a check-from-the-start routine. I made the call to stop building once the run was verified and to leave the fish untouched. That reduced the risk of late bumps and kept the table calm in the final minutes.

My honest view is that my hands-on building was a modest part of the total, and my main contribution was verification and coordination.", "my_share_percent": 20}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I took ownership of the bottom line of the fish, the longest single stroke on the pad, and laid it from the nose through the belly curve out to the tail. That was about 47 dominoes across several batches, roughly 40% of the 113 standing dominoes. The bottom contour is half of what the judge sees. It gives the body its belly and the tail its lower fork, so it was central to the fish reading as a fish. The finished run connected from the start through all 113 dominoes.

Execution: I picked up my stroke and worked it steadily and quietly, without needing direction. I traced it straight from the shared sketch, so the curves stayed smooth with no sharp corners. I used close inspections of my area at several points to check the chain was carrying through. When the run was complete, I stopped building so nothing got bumped before the push.

Collaboration: I worked in my own stretch of the table, away from where the others were laying the top line and tail. That kept us from bumping each other. I stuck to the plan agreed at the start, with Jack's sketch, my assigned bottom stroke and Sofia keeping the bin stocked. When the team agreed to keep hands off, I confirmed that and backed it.

Leadership: My leadership was by example. I took the assigned piece, delivered it cleanly and did not create extra work or confusion for the table. I kept the mood light and was positive in the final stretch. I helped the team hold discipline at the end by backing the hands-off call.

Overall, I believe the bottom line I built was a major part of the fish's recognizable outline, and I delivered it reliably.", "my_share_percent": 35}
